He also produced a widely used Quranic commentary and was one of the most prolific Ottoman legal writers of his era.

events.label: Köprülü Mehmed Pasha — Grand Vizier
events.description: Köprülü Mehmed Pasha was an Albanian-born devshirme official who, at age eighty-one in 1656, agreed to become grand vizier only after the court accepted his demand for nearly unlimited authority — full control of appointments, military operations, and finance, with no interference from the harem.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He ran the empire for five years by executing thousands of officials he judged corrupt or disloyal — a brutally effective if bloody approach to administrative reform. His son Fazıl Ahmed Pasha succeeded him and governed for another fifteen years, making the Köprülüs effectively a hereditary grand-vizieral dynasty. Together they gave the empire roughly a generation of competent central administration, during which the territorial losses of the chaotic mid-century were halted and some ground was recovered.

events.label: Nurbanu Sultan — Valide Sultan
events.description: Nurbanu Sultan was a Venetian-Greek noblewoman (born Cecilia Venier-Baffo on the island of Paros) who was captured by Ottoman corsairs as a teenager and rose through the harem to become the first truly politically dominant valide sultan (the sultan's mother) in Ottoman history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Her correspondence with Catherine de' Medici of France — two of the most powerful women of the 1570s — survives and shows her negotiating Ottoman-French relations directly, not through male intermediaries. She commissioned the Atik Valide Mosque complex in Istanbul, one of Mimar Sinan's last major works. Her Venetian origin was an open secret at the Ottoman court, and Venice cultivated the connection carefully, hoping it would soften Ottoman policy toward the Republic.

events.label: Kara Mustafa Pasha — Grand Vizier
events.description: Kara Mustafa Pasha was the grand vizier who assembled the largest Ottoman field army since Süleyman — roughly 120,000 men — and marched it to the walls of Vienna in 1683, gambling the empire's western momentum on a siege he ultimately lost.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Kara Mustafa delayed the final assault on Vienna's crumbling walls because he wanted to take the city intact rather than looted — a decision that gave the relief army time to arrive. After the defeat, he retreated to Belgrade, where on Christmas Day 1683 he was strangled with a silken bowstring (the standard Ottoman execution method for high officials) on Sultan Mehmed IV's orders; his head was sent to Istanbul as proof. The tent and treasure he abandoned at Vienna, reportedly worth millions, were distributed among the victorious allied commanders.

events.label: Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca
events.description: The 1774 Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca ended a six-year war the Ottomans lost decisively to Catherine the Great's Russia, ceding Black Sea territories and granting Russia the right to claim itself protector of the empire's Orthodox Christian subjects — a legal hook Russia would use to justify intervention in Ottoman affairs for the next century.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The treaty also gave Russia the right to build an Orthodox church in Istanbul and to make representations on its behalf — a small concession that Russian diplomats stretched into a near-unlimited mandate to interfere in Ottoman internal affairs. The practical loss of Crimea followed in 1783, stripping the Ottomans of the Tatar horse-warrior vassal state that had served as their northern buffer since the late fifteenth century.

events.label: Mustafa Reşid Pasha — Tanzimat Architect
events.description: Mustafa Reşid Pasha was the Ottoman diplomat-turned-statesman who drafted and personally read the Gülhane Rescript in 1839, serving six terms as grand vizier and driving the Tanzimat reform agenda until his death in 1858.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Reşid Pasha served as Ottoman ambassador in both Paris and London before drafting the Tanzimat reforms, making him unusually well-acquainted with European legal and administrative models. His repeated grand vizierate appointments — six in all — reflected both his indispensability and the political turbulence of the reform era, as conservative factions repeatedly forced him out and reformers repeatedly brought him back.

events.label: Enver Pasha — War Minister
events.description: The most militarily ambitious of the Three Pashas who ruled the empire 1913–1918 — War Minister Enver Pasha forged the German alliance, personally commanded the catastrophic winter offensive at Sarıkamış (1914) that destroyed the Ottoman Third Army, and died in 1922 fighting the Bolsheviks in Central Asia while trying to lead a pan-Turkic rebellion.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: At Sarıkamış, Enver personally commanded roughly 90,000 troops sent into the eastern Anatolian highlands in midwinter without adequate cold-weather equipment; the army lost perhaps three-quarters of its strength to combat, frostbite, and starvation in a matter of weeks. After fleeing Istanbul in 1918, Enver ended up in Soviet-controlled Central Asia — initially sent as a Bolshevik envoy — then defected and led the Basmachi resistance fighters against the Red Army in Bukhara until he was killed in a cavalry skirmish in 1922.

events.label: Talaat Pasha — Interior Minister
events.description: The most powerful of the Three Pashas, Talaat Pasha served as Interior Minister and later Grand Vizier; as the chief administrator of the 1915 deportation orders he bore primary institutional responsibility for the Armenian Genocide, and was assassinated in Berlin in 1921 by an Armenian survivor named Soghomon Tehlirian.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Talaat reportedly told American ambassador Morgenthau that the deportations were deliberate policy, not a security measure. His assassin Tehlirian was tried in a German court and acquitted — the jury accepted that Tehlirian had witnessed his own family's massacre and acted under temporary insanity. Turkey exhumed Talaat's remains from Berlin in 1943 and reinterred them in Istanbul as a state hero, a monument that still stands.

events.label: Mustafa Kemal (Atatürk)
events.description: Mustafa Kemal (1881–1938) — who took the surname Atatürk, meaning 'Father of the Turks,' in 1934 — was the Ottoman general who stopped the Anzac advance at Gallipoli, then led the nationalist war that expelled the Greek army from Anatolia, and finally dismantled every major Ottoman institution to build a secular, European-modeled republic.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He was born in Salonica (now Thessaloniki, Greece), a cosmopolitan port city full of minority communities — hardly the heartland Anatolian background his later image projected. He died in 1938 at Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul, and his physical remains were later moved to a specially built mausoleum in Ankara called Anıtkabir. After his death, the Turkish parliament passed a law making it a criminal offense to insult his memory — a law still on the books today.
